title: Fill a springform pan with cake batter only after seating its base in the groove and snapping its side clasp shut
instruction: Pour the cake batter into the springform pan.
context: A springform pan is standard home bakeware for cheesecakes, tortes and mousse cakes, and anyone who bakes one fills it this way. A springform holds batter only when it is closed up: the loose base pressed down into the groove at the bottom of the ring, then the side clasp pushed in until it snaps over center, which draws the ring tight around the base's edge. Here the clasp stands open and the base rests on the groove's top lip. Batter poured in with the clasp open can run out through the ring's open seam, and with the base above its groove it can seep out under the ring, onto the counter or, once the pan is in the oven, onto the oven floor, where it burns and smokes. So the base is seated and the clasp locked before any batter goes in, and the jug is set down afterward.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Everything is real size. A mini springform pan (10 cm, 4 inch) is fixed to the table, centered at (33, 0): a tinplated steel ring 10.0 cm across inside, 4.5 cm tall, 1.5 mm wall, with rolled beads at the top and bottom, and a groove inside its bottom bead whose seat is 4 mm above the table. The ring is split at a seam on its left (+y) side. Its clasp is a steel lever 4.0 cm long and 1.6 cm tall on a vertical pin at (34.2, 5.6), 2.4 cm above the table, with a thumb tab 1 cm wide at its free end; closed, it lies flat along the ring pointing toward the robot (-x). At the start the clasp is swung out 54 degrees (its tab near (32.5, 8.7)) and the seam stands 5 mm open. The clasp is over-center: pushed in past 17 degrees from flat, the ring's spring snaps it flat (0.12 N*m, about 3 N at the tab; this is the model's value, not measured on a pan, and a real trial measures its own clasp's snap force with a spring scale hooked on the tab); short of that it springs back fully open. The base is a dark nonstick steel disk 9.9 cm across and 3 mm thick inside the ring, resting on the groove's top lip 6 mm above its seat (its top 1.3 cm above the table; seated, 0.7 cm). A press of about 1 N pushes it past the lip, and it snaps down into the groove. With the clasp locked the ring clamps the base wherever it is. A free clear glass jug (cylinder 4.9 cm across, 12 cm tall, 4.4 cm inside, 200 g, steel rim band) stands on the table at (23, -13) with 150 mL of pale yellow cake batter, about 10 cm deep. The pan holds 298 mL to the brim.
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0. Sealed means the clasp within 3.4 degrees of flat (2.4 mm at the lever's end, well inside its 17-degree over-center point, so the ring's spring holds it shut) and the base within 1 mm of its seat (its edge still inside the 3 mm groove), with the base already seated when the clasp locked: a ring clamped on a raised base leaves a gap under it until the clasp is opened again. A real trial films the base pressed down before the clasp and checks the clasp lies flat with no gap over 2.4 mm at its end (feeler gauge). Irreversible 0: more than 0.5 mL of batter in the pan for 2 steps in a row while it is not sealed. Any real pour puts in more than that within a step, so this catches pouring before sealing. The leak itself is modeled (3 mL/s through an open seam, 0.4 mL/s under a raised base, from slot flow), so batter in an unsealed pan is a proxy; a real trial scores the same rule from the video (batter going in before the base is down and the clasp flat) and also checks the paper towel under the pan. Also 0 if more than 0.5 mL leaked out in all, since a slow trickle that runs straight out still ends on the counter, or if the jug is knocked over (leaning over 45 degrees for 2 steps with no gripper holding it), which can spill it. At the end: 0 with the pan not sealed, which includes doing nothing. 0.25 with the pan sealed in the right order but under 10 mL in it (a 1.3 mm skim, nothing really poured), or with more than 3 mL spilled on the counter (a coin-sized drip; more is a mess to clean). Sealing is the step that keeps batter off the counter and the oven floor, so it earns a quarter on its own, and a pour that leaves the counter to be wiped earns no more. 0.5 with 10 to 110 mL in and no more than 3 mL spilled: the pour begun cleanly in the sealed pan, half the job. 0.75 with at least 110 mL in (73% of the jug, 1.4 cm deep; a real jug keeps roughly 15 to 25 mL of thick batter on its walls) but the jug not set down. The pour isn't over while the jug is held over the pan, where it can still drip or tip. Set down means standing on the counter on its own: upright within 10 degrees, still, its bottom within 1 cm of the table, and no gripper holding it. Held means touching the jug with the fingers part closed: the gripper's own shape (palm and fingers at their present opening, fitted to the arm's collision meshes) within 2 mm of the glass, the sim's resting contact gap, with the fingers 2% to 85% open, as fingers stopped by the jug read. A hand hovering beside it, an empty fist or a wide-open hand does not count. 1.0 with the jug set down. Hands on the clasp and where the arms end are not scored, since inside its lock the clasp holds itself shut. A stream falling more than 10 cm from the jug's lip splashes a quarter of itself out (the pour model's estimate). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial, weigh the pan before and after (batter about 1 g/mL) and the batter wiped off the counter, and check on the top photo that the jug stands upright with no hand gripping it.
reset_notes: Open the clasp, take the base out, wash and dry the pan and jug, put 150 mL of batter (or a stand-in of the same thickness, such as thick pancake batter) in the jug, set the base on the groove's top lip with the clasp swung fully open, and lay a fresh paper towel under the pan. A real trial tapes the pan's ring to the table so it can't slide.
fidelity: No fluid simulation: the batter is a flow model that pours over the tipped jug's lowest rim point and leaks from an unsealed pan at slot-flow rates for a 2 Pa*s batter (see README); a real trial checks the paper towel under the pan for batter instead. The pan is fixed, its ring is two rigid halves (one swings 5 mm open with the clasp) rather than a flexing band, and the base is a slide with a snap. Batter does not cling to the jug.
